197.title: Vayishlach: three ways to prepare
197.hook: Rashi: Jacob readied gifts, prayer and defense before meeting Esau
197.howItsDone: Jewish teachers often cite Rashi's three preparations, gift, prayer and defense, as a guide for facing conflict, and the chapter is read each late autumn in Vayishlach.

segments.voice: Yesterday, katonti: Jacob's prayer, too small for all this kindness. Did you name a kindness before asking? Today, the night before the meeting, Jacob gets ready. Day one hundred ninety-seven.

The night before the big interview. The surgery. The hard talk with your landlord, or your father. Some people only worry. Some people only pray. Some people only make spreadsheets. Jacob has a brother coming toward him with four hundred men, and one night to get ready. And if you read the chapter closely, he does three very different things. The rabbis noticed the pattern and gave it a name. Today: three ways to prepare.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE.` → `WORRY, PRAY, OR PLAN?` → `JACOB DOES THREE THINGS.`

segments.voice: Rashi, reading this chapter, says Jacob prepared himself for three things: for a gift, for prayer, and for war. Take them one at a time. War, or really, defense. Jacob divides his people and flocks into two camps. If Esau attacks one, the other can escape. He isn't planning to fight his brother. He's planning so that not everyone is lost. Prayer. We heard it yesterday: God of my fathers, I'm too small for all your kindness, save me, I'm afraid. And a gift. This is the part people forget. Jacob sets aside hundreds of animals. Goats and sheep, rams, camels with their young, cows and bulls, donkeys. He sends them ahead in separate droves, each with its own servant, and tells them: put space between one drove and the next. So Esau meets gift after gift after gift, each servant saying, this is a present for my lord Esau, from your servant Jacob. The Hebrew word for the gift is minchah, the same word as the afternoon prayer, Mincha. A gift to a brother and a gift to God share a name. Jacob explains his plan in a phrase that's hard to translate. Literally: I will cover his face with the gift. Some hear in it the same root as kapparah, atonement, the covering-over of a wrong. Jacob isn't only buying safety. He's trying to repay, a little, what he took twenty years ago. Rashi's three ways became a model. When facing something hard, don't choose only one. Be generous. Pray, if you pray. And be practical.
screen: `A GIFT, PRAYER, AND DEFENSE.` · `TWO CAMPS, SO SOME ESCAPE.` · `SPACE BETWEEN THE DROVES.` · `MINCHAH: A GIFT, AND A PRAYER.` · then, large: `PREPARE THREE WAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: prepare three ways for one hard thing. Settle, and breathe. Pick one hard thing coming up this week. First, the practical way: one sensible step you could take. Second, the generous way: one gift, or kind word, you could offer the other person. Third, the way of prayer: if you pray, bring it to God; if you don't, take one quiet breath with it. Let all three sit together. The bell holds the time.
Vayishlach. And he sent: the portion where Jacob sends gift after gift ahead of him, and prepares with gifts, prayer and defense.
Your line: prepare three ways. Today, for one hard thing ahead, do something practical, something generous, and something quiet. Day one hundred ninety-seven.

198.title: Vayishlach: the limp (Genesis 32:32–33)
198.hook: Jacob limps from the wrestling, and Jews still avoid eating the sinew of the thigh
198.howItsDone: Kosher butchers remove the gid hanasheh, the sciatic nerve, from the hindquarter in a skilled process called nikkur, and in many places outside Israel the hindquarters are simply not sold as kosher.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a gift, a prayer and two camps. Your line was prepare three ways. How did you get ready for something hard? Today, what happened that night. Day one hundred ninety-eight.

Everybody has one. The scar on your knee from the bike. The shoulder that aches when it rains. The wrist that never quite healed right. You forget about it for months, and then one cold morning it reminds you of a day you'd almost forgotten. The night before meeting Esau, Jacob is alone by the river Jabbok, and a man wrestles with him until dawn. Jacob won't let go without a blessing, and he walks away with a new name, Israel. He also walks away with something else. Today: the limp.
screen: `THE SCAR THAT ACHES IN THE RAIN.` → `WRESTLING UNTIL DAWN.` → `A NEW NAME, AND SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: During the struggle, the man touched the hollow of Jacob's thigh, and it was wrenched. Jacob names the place Peniel, face of God, because, he says, I have seen God face to face, and I'm still alive. And then the Torah gives us a picture. The sun rose on him as he passed Peniel, and he was limping on his thigh. Morning light, a new name, and a limp. He isn't the same man who crossed the river. Then the Torah does something unusual. It steps out of the story to speak to the future. Therefore, it says, the children of Israel don't eat the sinew of the thigh, on the hollow of the thigh, to this day, because he touched Jacob's thigh there. In Hebrew, that sinew is the gid hanasheh. Many identify it with the sciatic nerve, which runs down the back of the leg. And the practice is real. Jewish law forbids eating it, and there's a whole chapter of the Mishnah about it. Removing it from the hindquarter of an animal is slow, skilled work. In many places outside Israel, kosher butchers find it simpler not to use the hindquarters at all. So a detail from one night by a river still shapes what's on the table, three thousand years of dinners later. Why remember the limp, and not only the victory? A medieval book on the commandments says it's a sign: Jacob struggled, was hurt, and wasn't defeated. His children would struggle too, and endure. The limp isn't a shame to hide. It's a memory the body keeps, on purpose, so the story doesn't get lost.
screen: `THE HOLLOW OF THE THIGH, WRENCHED.` · `PENIEL: FACE OF GOD.` · `THE SUN ROSE ON A LIMPING MAN.` · `GID HANASHEH, TO THIS DAY.` · then, large: `THE LIMP REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor one old scar. Settle, and breathe. Find a scar on your body, or one that doesn't show: a loss, a failure, a hard year. Put your hand on it if you can. Remember the night it came from. You wrestled. You were hurt. And you're still here. Don't rush to fix the memory. Let it be part of your story, the way the limp is part of Jacob's. The bell holds the time.
Gid hanasheh. The sinew of the thigh, which Jews don't eat, in memory of Jacob's limp after he wrestled until dawn.
Your line: the limp remembers. Today, when an old hurt twinges, instead of pushing it away, remember that you came through it. Day one hundred ninety-eight.

199.title: Vayishlach: back to Bethel (Genesis 35:1–15)
199.hook: Jacob buries the old idols and returns to where he dreamed
199.howItsDone: Jewish tradition treats fulfilling vows seriously, and on Yom Kippur eve the Kol Nidre service opens by addressing unfulfilled vows; Jacob's return to Bethel is read in Vayishlach each late autumn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gid hanasheh, and Jacob limping into the sunrise. Your line was the limp remembers. Did an old hurt remind you of something? Today, Jacob goes back to where it started. Day one hundred ninety-nine.

Maybe you've done this. Driven past the house you grew up in. Walked into the old school gym, or the hospital chapel where you once made a promise. The place looks smaller. You're older. And you remember who you were, and what you said you'd do. Jacob has met Esau, and they've embraced and gone their separate ways. His family has been through a violent, painful chapter in the town of Shechem. And now God speaks: go up to Bethel. The place of the ladder. Today: back to Bethel.
screen: `THE HOUSE YOU GREW UP IN.` → `A HARD CHAPTER AT SHECHEM.` → `GO UP TO BETHEL.`

segments.voice: God says: go up to Bethel, live there, and make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother. Remember that night? The stone for a pillow, the ladder, the vow. Jacob doesn't just pack. First, he turns to his household and says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Put away the strange gods that are among you." Purify yourselves, change your clothes. Wait. Strange gods? In Jacob's camp? The Torah has been hinting. When the family left Laban's house, Rachel secretly took her father's household idols. After Shechem there was plunder, too. Somewhere in all those tents and saddlebags, the old gods came along. So the family hands them over, the idols and the earrings they wore, and Jacob buries them under the great tree near Shechem. He doesn't smash them in public. He buries them, and leaves them behind. Then they go up. Along the way Deborah, Rebekah's old nurse, dies, and they bury her under an oak they name the oak of weeping. At Bethel, God appears again, blesses Jacob, and repeats his new name: Israel. And Jacob does exactly what he did twenty years before. He sets up a stone pillar and pours oil on it. Same place, same stone ritual, different man. The rabbis read Bethel as the promise kept. Jacob vowed there, if God would bring him home in peace. Now he's back, keeping his side. But first, he had to bury what he'd been carrying that didn't belong.
screen: `GO UP TO BETHEL.` · `PUT AWAY THE STRANGE GODS.` · `BURIED UNDER THE TREE.` · `THE SAME STONE, A DIFFERENT MAN.` · then, large: `BURY THE OLD GODS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go back to a place of promise. Settle, and breathe. Remember a place where you once made a promise, to yourself, to someone you love, or, if you pray, to God. See it clearly. Now ask what you've picked up since then that doesn't belong on the way back. An old habit, a grudge, something you worship that isn't worth it. Picture burying it under a tree, and walking on. The bell holds the time.
Vayishlach. And he sent: the portion where Jacob buries the old gods under a tree and goes back up to Bethel, where he dreamed.
Your line: bury the old gods. Today, put away one thing you've been carrying that doesn't belong, and don't dig it back up. Day one hundred ninety-nine.

200.title: Vayishlach: Esau's family (Genesis 35:29–36:43)
200.hook: the brothers bury Isaac together, and Esau's descendants are listed with care
200.howItsDone: The genealogy of Esau is read aloud in synagogues each year as part of Vayishlach, every name included, and Jewish teachers often point to Deuteronomy's command not to abhor an Edomite.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bethel, and a family burying its idols under a tree. Your line was bury the old gods. What did you put down? Day two hundred. Two hundred days on the path. Today, a chapter most people skip.

At a family reunion, there's always the other side. Your cousins from your uncle's marriage, the ones you see once every five years. Different town, different jokes, different photos on the fridge. You're polite. You don't really know their story. Genesis 36 is that other side of the family. It's a long list of names, and most readers' eyes slide right over it. But it comes right after a funeral, and it's there on purpose. Today: Esau's family.
screen: `THE OTHER SIDE OF THE FAMILY.` → `GENESIS 36: A LIST OF NAMES.` → `THERE ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: First, the funeral. Isaac dies at a hundred and eighty, old and full of days. And the text says his sons Esau and Jacob buried him. Remember, when Abraham died, Isaac was named before Ishmael. Here the older brother, Esau, comes first. The two brothers who fought in the womb, who fought over a blessing, stand together at their father's grave. Then the Torah turns, not to Jacob, but to Esau. These are the generations of Esau, who is Edom. His wives, his sons, his grandsons. It tells us Esau moved his whole household to the hill country of Seir, because the land couldn't hold both brothers' flocks. No war, no curse. They just needed room. Then come chiefs, and a list of the kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over Israel. Esau's family had kings first. The Torah says so, calmly. One name in the list caught the rabbis' eye: Timna. The Talmud tells a story about her. She wanted to join Abraham's family, and was turned away, so she became the concubine of Esau's son instead, and from her descended Amalek, later one of Israel's bitterest enemies. The rabbis' lesson: be careful whom you push away. Later, the Torah itself says it plainly, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite, for he is thy brother." God gave Esau his land too, Deuteronomy says, and Israel was told not to fight over it. A whole chapter, for the brother who wasn't chosen. Every name written down with care. His story matters too.
screen: `ESAU AND JACOB BURY ISAAC.` · `THE GENERATIONS OF ESAU.` · `KINGS IN EDOM FIRST.` · `DO NOT ABHOR AN EDOMITE.` · then, large: `HIS STORY MATTERS TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect a family that isn't yours. Settle, and breathe. Picture a family you tend to overlook. Your in-laws. The neighbors with different customs. The side of the family you don't call. Imagine their list of names: grandparents, children, the people they've buried, the ones they're proud of. Let their story become as real as yours for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Vayishlach. And he sent: the portion that ends with the brothers burying Isaac, and a whole chapter for Esau's family.
Your line: his story matters too. Today, ask someone from another family, another background, one question about their people, and really listen to the answer. Day two hundred.

201.title: Vayeshev: wanting to settle (Genesis 37:1)
201.hook: Rashi: Jacob wished to live in peace, and Joseph's troubles sprang upon him
201.howItsDone: Vayeshev is read in synagogues in early winter, often near Hanukkah, and Rashi's comment on Jacob's wish for tranquility is one of the best-known in the Joseph story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a whole chapter for Esau's family. Your line was his story matters too. Whose story did you listen to? Today, a new portion, and Jacob wants to sit down. Day two hundred one.

You know the feeling. The move is done, the boxes are unpacked, the kids are finally sleeping through the night, and you sit down on the couch and think: now, finally, things can be calm. And that's usually when the phone rings. Jacob has had a life like a storm. A brother who wanted him dead. Twenty years with a difficult uncle. Wrestling, limping, burying his mother's nurse, and his beloved Rachel. Now he's home. This portion is called Vayeshev, and he settled. Today: wanting to settle.
screen: `FINALLY, THE COUCH.` → `A LIFE LIKE A STORM.` → `VAYESHEV: AND HE SETTLED.`

segments.voice: The portion opens with a quiet verse. Jacob settled in the land of his father's sojournings, in the land of Canaan. Notice the two verbs. His father Isaac sojourned there, lived like a guest. Jacob wants to settle, to sit down, to stay. The very next verse starts the story of Joseph: a seventeen-year-old, a favorite son, a coat, some dreams, and brothers who hate him. Within a chapter, Joseph is gone and Jacob is tearing his clothes in grief. Rashi, reading those two verses side by side, drew on an old midrash. Jacob wished to dwell in tranquility, he says, and the troubles of Joseph sprang upon him. Rashi even adds a sharp line: the righteous want to live at ease in this world too, and God says, isn't what's waiting for them in the world to come enough? That can sound harsh. But hear it another way. Rashi isn't mocking the wish for peace. Everyone wants it. He's noticing a pattern in the text, and in life: calm is real, but it isn't a place you move into and own. It comes, and it goes. Jacob's hardest years are still ahead of him, and some of his sweetest too. In the end, he'll see Joseph again. The Hebrew word here, vayeshev, comes from the same root as yeshivah, a place where you sit and study, and as the word for sitting in a home. Jewish life has plenty of sitting: at the Shabbat table, in study, even in mourning, sitting shivah. Rest is holy. It's just never guaranteed.
screen: `HIS FATHER SOJOURNED; HE SETTLED.` · `THE TROUBLES OF JOSEPH SPRANG.` · `CALM COMES, AND GOES.` · `YESHIVAH, SHIVAH: SITTING.` · then, large: `REST COMES AND GOES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept that calm isn't guaranteed. Settle, and breathe. Notice any calm there is right now, even a little. The chair holding you. The quiet in the room, or the noise you've gotten used to. Enjoy it fully, without clutching. Then let yourself know that it will change, and that you've come through changes before. Hold both: this rest is real, and it doesn't have to last forever to be good. The bell holds the time.
Vayeshev. And he settled: the portion where Jacob finally sits down, and the troubles of Joseph begin.
Your line: rest comes and goes. Today, when a calm moment comes, enjoy it on purpose, and when it's interrupted, let it go without a fight. Day two hundred one.

202.title: Vayeshev: the man in the field (Genesis 37:15–17)
202.hook: a nameless stranger points Joseph to his brothers; midrash calls him an angel
202.howItsDone: Joseph's words, et achai anochi mevakesh, I seek my brothers, are often quoted in Jewish teaching and song as a call to look for and care for one another.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vayeshev: Jacob wanting to settle, and trouble springing up. Your line was rest comes and goes. Did you enjoy a calm moment on purpose? Day two hundred two.

You're lost in a new city. Your phone is dead. You've walked the same block three times. And then someone, an old man at a bus stop, a kid on a bike, asks: you look lost, where are you trying to go? Two sentences later, you're on your way, and you never see them again. Joseph's brothers are far from home, grazing the flocks. Jacob sends Joseph, alone, to check on them. He goes to Shechem, where they were supposed to be. They aren't there. Today: the man in the field.
screen: `LOST, PHONE DEAD.` → `SENT TO FIND HIS BROTHERS.` → `THEY AREN'T THERE.`

segments.voice: The Torah says a man found Joseph wandering in the field. Just, a man. No name. And the man asks, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "What seekest thou?" Joseph answers with a line that has become famous in Hebrew: et achai anochi mevakesh. "I seek my brethren." Tell me, please, where they're pasturing. And the stranger says: they've moved on. I heard them say, let's go to Dothan. So Joseph goes to Dothan. And there the brothers see him coming, and the story turns. The pit, the caravan, Egypt, everything that follows starts with a stranger who knew where they'd gone. Why does the Torah bother with him? Three verses for a man with no name, who asks one question and gives one answer. The rabbis couldn't leave it alone. An old midrash, which Rashi quotes, says the man was the angel Gabriel. Ramban, in medieval Spain, said: whether or not he was an angel, the point is that Joseph's story had to happen, and when Joseph was about to give up and go home, someone was put in his path. Others read him as simply a passerby, which may be the point too. The text itself doesn't say who he was. It only tells us that at the moment Joseph was lost, somebody noticed, asked, and pointed. Most of the turning points in our lives have a figure like that. A teacher who mentioned a book. A stranger who gave a name, a number, a direction. We rarely know their names. Often we never thank them.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a stranger who helped you. Settle, and breathe. Think back to a time you were lost, in a city, a job, a hard year. Was there someone who pointed the way? Maybe you knew their name, maybe you didn't. Picture their face if you can. Say thank you to them, silently, now. If you pray, you can thank God for putting them in your path. The bell holds the time.
Vayeshev. And he settled: the portion where a nameless man in a field points Joseph to his brothers, and the whole story turns.
Your line: someone points the way. Today, be that someone once: notice a person who looks lost, and ask what they're looking for. Day two hundred two.

203.title: Vayeshev: the empty pit (Genesis 37:24)
203.hook: "the pit was empty, there was no water in it"
203.howItsDone: The sale of Joseph is read in synagogues each winter in Vayeshev, and later Jewish tradition links the brothers' sin to the martyrdom of ten sages remembered on Yom Kippur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man with no name who pointed Joseph to Dothan. Your line was someone points the way. This week: three ways to prepare, a limp, back to Bethel, Esau's family, wanting to settle, and the man in the field. Today, what waited at Dothan. Day two hundred three.

Some moments in life are just a hole. A diagnosis. A layoff. The night the house goes quiet after a divorce. You're at the bottom of something, and you can't see a way up. Joseph walks toward his brothers across the fields at Dothan, wearing the coat his father gave him. They see him coming from far off. And before he reaches them, they've already made a plan. Today: the empty pit.
screen: `AT THE BOTTOM OF SOMETHING.` → `THE COAT, SEEN FROM FAR OFF.` → `A PLAN BEFORE HE ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: The brothers say: here comes the dreamer. Let's kill him, throw him into one of the pits, and say a wild animal ate him. Then we'll see what becomes of his dreams. Reuben, the oldest, steps in. Don't take his life. Throw him into this pit, here in the wilderness, but don't lay a hand on him. The Torah tells us why: Reuben meant to come back later and rescue him. So Joseph arrives, and they strip off his coat, the coat, and throw him into the pit. And then the Torah gives us one flat detail, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "and the pit was empty, there was no water in it." Why tell us that? If it's empty, of course there's no water. The rabbis read the doubled phrase slowly. The Talmud says: there was no water in it, but there were snakes and scorpions. Empty of what helps, and not empty of what harms. Others hear it more plainly. A dry pit meant Joseph wouldn't drown. It was a cistern for catching rain, and it was dry. Empty can be terrible. It can also be the thing that keeps you alive. And then the next verse, one of the coldest in the Torah. The brothers sat down to eat bread. Their brother is in a hole a few steps away, and they have lunch. The story doesn't let us look away from that. Joseph is in the pit, stripped, alone. Nothing in it but darkness. And, the story will show, it isn't the end of him.
